Both are presidential letters urging congressional action on a negotiated bilateral agreement: each recounts the foreign-government negotiations or position, explains why congressional authorization is necessary, argues that the arrangement benefits the United States and its bilateral relations, and closes with an emphatic request for legislation. C12 and C19 concern foreign economic policy and congressional action but lack this close bilateral-agreement structure.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"Discussions on specific Philippine proposals for revision began last September ... and culminated in the signing ... of a Final Act of Negotiations","parent_excerpt":"The Canadians agree with us that the quickest and most desirable way to get started on the project is for the Congress to approve the joint development plan now before it.","explanation":"Both letters use the outcome of bilateral discussions as the immediate basis for requesting congressional approval."},{"child_excerpt":"Revision of the 1946 Agreement cannot be effected without the authorization of the Congress.","parent_excerpt":"That can only be done if the Congress acts.","explanation":"The same operative premise organizes both letters: implementation of an international arrangement depends on congressional authorization."},{"child_excerpt":"I earnestly urge, therefore, that appropriate legislation be enacted at this session of the Congress","parent_excerpt":"I strongly recommend that your committee and the Congress promptly complete action on this vital matter.","explanation":"Both conclude with a direct, urgent appeal for Congress to enact or complete the necessary legislation."}]}
